title: 07 · Extra Credit: Non-Identical Bernoulli Shots
text:
1 Research Question
Does a normal approximation emerge similarly when observations remain independent but are not identically distributed?

title: 07 · Extra Credit: Non-Identical Bernoulli Shots
text:
2 Population / Process and Theory
For each candidate n, probabilities p_i are evenly spaced from 0.90 to 0.50, and X_i ~ Bernoulli(p_i) independently. The theoretical mean of the average is (1/n) * sum(p_i). The variance is sum(p_i * (1 - p_i)) / n^2, not an iid Binomial calculation.

title: 07 · Extra Credit: Non-Identical Bernoulli Shots
text:
3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
Independence and finite variance hold, while identical distribution does not. Since the probabilities vary smoothly and stay away from 0 and 1, a normal approximation may be reasonable, but the relevant mean and variance change with candidate n.

title: 05 · Cauchy
text:
1 Research Question
What does increasing n do when the population is Cauchy and has no finite population mean or variance?

title: 05 · Cauchy
text:
2 Population / Process and Theory
X_i ~ Cauchy(location = 0, scale = 1). The population mean and variance do not exist. This project therefore does not report a population mean, population SD, or sigma / sqrt(n) for this case.

title: 05 · Cauchy
text:
3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
Independence and identical distribution hold, but finite variance fails. I expect extreme observations to remain influential and ordinary mean-based normal convergence to behave differently from the finite-variance cases.

title: 05 · Cauchy
text:
5 Final Selected N and Interpretation

Code
report_selection(spec$id)

Selected N: No finite defensible value identified within the tested range.
Evidence decision: No finite defensible n was identified through n = 5,000; Cauchy has no population mean or variance and the running mean remains extreme-sensitive.
The N/A decision is limited to this ordinary sample-mean criterion and the tested range through n = 5,000; it is not a claim that every possible robust estimator fails. The project correctly leaves population mean, population SD, and sigma / sqrt(n) as N/A.

1 Research Question
How much averaging is needed to overcome the strong right skew of an Exponential(rate = 1) population?

title: 03 · Exponential

2 Population / Process and Theory
X_i ~ Exponential(rate = 1), with mean 1, standard deviation 1, and theoretical SE 1 / sqrt(n).

title: 03 · Exponential

3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
The observations are iid and have finite variance, so the ordinary CLT applies. I expect the right tail and positive skewness to be visible for small n, with empirical SE approaching 1 / sqrt(n) as n grows.

title: 01 · Standard Normal
text:
1 Research Question
How well do simulation diagnostics behave when the population is already Normal?

title: 01 · Standard Normal
text:
2 Population / Process and Theory
X_i ~ N(0, 1). Because Normal distributions are closed under averaging, the sample mean is exactly N(0, 1/n) for every positive integer n, including n = 1.

title: 01 · Standard Normal
text:
3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
The observations are independent, identically distributed, and have finite variance. I expect all diagnostics to fluctuate around their theoretical targets at every tested n; those fluctuations quantify Monte Carlo noise.

The choice n = 1 is theoretical, not a claim that simulation detected a transition: a Normal population has an exactly Normal sample mean for every positive n.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
1 Research question
What is the smallest sample size (n) at which I would be comfortable calling the sampling distribution of the sample mean approximately normal? This project treats that as an evidence-based judgment, not a universal theorem with one answer.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
2 Is (n=30) a universal rule?
No. The generated evidence shows that n = 30 is context-dependent: it is enough for the exactly Normal benchmark and already persuasive for the synthetic age mixture, but it leaves visible skewness or Q-Q deviations for the Exponential, small-probability Binomial, and non-identical Bernoulli cases. Cauchy and the dependent failure process do not receive a defensible finite selection under the tested criteria.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
4 What the results say
The fastest cases were Standard Normal (exactly normal for every n) and the synthetic age-at-death mixture. The die was also close to normal by n = 100. The slower finite-variance cases were the Exponential and Binomial(size = 5, p = 0.10), where strong right skew and rare-event discreteness required n = 1,000 in this study. The non-identical Bernoulli process used the correct p_i-specific variance and reached its most persuasive tested evidence at n = 1,000.
The most important exception was Cauchy: even at n = 5,000, Q-Q RMSE stayed around 1.3 with extreme skewness and kurtosis, and the running mean remained sensitive to outliers. The dependent failure process improved as n grew but still showed positive skewness and Q-Q error above the Normal calibration through n = 1,000; its covariance structure means the iid SE formula is not appropriate.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
5 Reproducibility
The complete workflow is in README.md. The confirmed student seed is 7616 in R/config.R. The runner also repeats the boundary evidence with seed 7617; exact diagnostics move modestly, but the scientific pattern is stable. The instructor source documents are preserved under references/.

title: Methodology
text:
For a candidate sample size n, one repetition generates n observations and computes one sample mean. Repeating this B = 10,000 times produces the simulated sampling distribution of the sample mean.
The project uses a coarse-to-fine search. The initial grid is deliberately broad. After the coarse run is inspected, a human-selected transition center can be entered in R/config.R; the runner then adds nearby values for a refined search. No selected n is inferred solely from a p-value or hard-coded in the code.

title: Methodology
text:
For a candidate sample size n, one repetition generates n observations and computes one sample mean. Repeating this B = 10,000 times produces the simulated sampling distribution of the sample mean.
The project uses a coarse-to-fine search. The initial grid is deliberately broad. After the coarse run is inspected, a human-selected transition center can be entered in R/config.R; the runner then adds nearby values for a refined search. No selected n is inferred solely from a p-value or hard-coded in the code.

title: Methodology
text:
2 Evidence used together
Each candidate sample size is assessed with a histogram, a theoretical normal overlay when appropriate, a normal Q-Q plot, skewness, excess kurtosis, empirical mean, empirical SE, theoretical mean and SE where valid, and qq_rmse.
The Standard Normal population is simulated repeatedly as a calibration benchmark. Its diagnostic ranges show how much skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q RMSE can fluctuate at B = 10,000 even when the sampling distribution is exactly normal. This benchmark contextualizes, rather than mechanically decides, the other cases.

title: Methodology
text:
3 Assumptions and exceptions
The ordinary iid finite-variance CLT does not apply unchanged to every case. Cauchy has no population mean or variance. The dependent failure process requires covariance terms in the variance of a mean. The basketball process is independent but non-identically distributed and uses the variance formula sum(p_i * (1 - p_i)) / n^2, not an iid shortcut.
The age-at-death population is synthetic and uses the instructor-provided discrete mixture exactly; it is not historical mortality data.

title: Methodology
text:
4 Decision rule
The final selected n, when one exists, is the smallest tested value at which the evidence is jointly persuasive: the histogram is reasonably bell-shaped, the Q-Q plot lacks substantial systematic curvature, diagnostics are reasonably close to the Normal benchmark, theory agrees with simulation where applicable, and the conclusion remains stable at nearby larger values. The final report must state uncertainty and limitations.

title: Methodology
text:
5 Sensitivity to the random seed
The primary run uses the confirmed student seed 7616. The pipeline repeats the same simulation design with seed 7617 and stores those rows in results/sensitivity_diagnostics.csv. Exact skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q RMSE values move because they are Monte Carlo estimates, but the broad conclusions are not seed-shopped: the exact Normal case remains exact in theory, Cauchy remains highly unstable through n = 5,000, and the slower finite-variance cases remain slower than the die and age mixture.
The final selections are recorded in results/final_summary.csv by scripts/finalize_summary.R. That script checks that every finite selected value is an actual tested row before copying its generated diagnostics into the summary.

title: 02 · Six-Sided Die
text:
1 Research Question
How quickly does averaging a discrete uniform die produce a sampling distribution that is comfortable to call approximately normal?

title: 02 · Six-Sided Die
text:
2 Population / Process and Theory
X_i is uniform on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. The theoretical mean is 3.5, variance is 35/12, and the theoretical SE is sqrt(35/12) / sqrt(n).

title: 02 · Six-Sided Die
text:
3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
The draws are iid with finite variance, so the ordinary CLT applies. Symmetry should reduce skewness, while discreteness may remain visible at small n.

title: 02 · Six-Sided Die
text:
5 Final Selected N and Interpretation

Code
report_selection(spec$id)

Selected N: n = 100

skewness: 0.0207
excess kurtosis: -0.0238
Q-Q RMSE: 0.0209
empirical SE: 0.1713
theoretical/reference SE: 0.1708 Evidence decision: At n = 100, skewness and excess kurtosis are near zero, SE agrees with theory, and the Q-Q diagnostic is close to the calibrated range; larger nearby values are stable.

The die is bounded, symmetric, and finite-variance, so it converges much faster than strongly skewed or heavy-tailed populations. The selected value is the first reviewed value whose graphical and numerical evidence was persuasive together with nearby stability.
Use symmetry, discreteness, benchmark-calibrated diagnostics, theoretical SE agreement, and stability at neighboring values together. Do not infer the answer from one p-value.

title: 04 · Binomial Small
text:
1 Research Question
Does the CLT behave differently when each observation is a small, highly discrete Binomial count with a low success probability?

title: 04 · Binomial Small
text:
2 Population / Process and Theory
Y_i ~ Binomial(size = 5, p = 0.10). The Binomial parameter size = 5 is not the CLT sample size n. Here E[Y_i] = 0.5, Var(Y_i) = 0.45, and the iid theoretical SE is sqrt(0.45) / sqrt(n).

title: 04 · Binomial Small
text:
3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
The draws are iid with finite variance, so the ordinary CLT applies. The low mean and discreteness may keep the sampling distribution lumpy and right-skewed at modest n.

title: 04 · Binomial Small
text:
5 Final Selected N and Interpretation

Code
report_selection(spec$id)

Selected N: n = 1,000

skewness: 0.0237
excess kurtosis: 0.0246
Q-Q RMSE: 0.0176
empirical SE: 0.021
theoretical/reference SE: 0.0212 Evidence decision: The rare-event Binomial is slower than the die; n = 1,000 gives near-benchmark Q-Q error, small shape diagnostics, and agreement with sqrt(0.45 / n).

The selected value reflects the rare-event discreteness of Binomial(size = 5, p = 0.10). Here Binomial size = 5 is a distribution parameter; it is not the CLT sample size n. The theoretical SE is sqrt(0.45 / n) and agrees with the generated n = 1,000 result.

title: 06 · Extra Credit: Dependent Failure Process
text:
1 Research Question
How does the sampling distribution of a mean change when each operating time depends on the previous operating time?

title: 06 · Extra Credit: Dependent Failure Process
text:
2 Population / Process and Theory
The instructor model sets the next failure rate to baseline_rate * exp(beta * (previous_time - reference_time)), then draws the next operating time conditionally from an Exponential distribution. The supplied values are baseline rate 1, beta = 1.25, and reference time 1. A long operating period tends to be followed by a shorter one, creating compensating dependence.

title: 06 · Extra Credit: Dependent Failure Process
text:
3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
Observations are not independent and are not one fixed iid exponential distribution. The variance of a mean includes covariance terms, so the iid sigma / sqrt(n) formula is not used as if it were valid.

Evidence decision: No defensible n was identified through n = 1,000; dependence and persistent positive skew make the ordinary iid SE shortcut inappropriate.
Through n = 1,000, the process improves but still has positive skewness and Q-Q error above the Normal calibration. The N/A is therefore a tested-range decision, not a claim that no dependent-process CLT could ever be proved. The lag plot and negative lag-1 association also show why an iid standard-error shortcut is unsafe.

title: 08 · Extra Credit: Synthetic Age-at-Death
text:
1 Research Question
How does an irregular, bimodal-looking synthetic population behave after averaging?

title: 08 · Extra Credit: Synthetic Age-at-Death
text:
2 Population / Process and Theory
The instructor construction uses ages 0 through 100 with weights 0.045 * exp(-x/5) + 0.030 * exp(-0.5 * ((x - 65) / 10)^2), normalized to probabilities. The supplied rdeath() logic samples from those probabilities. The resulting distribution is synthetic, not historical mortality data; its mean and SD are computed from the normalized table.

title: 08 · Extra Credit: Synthetic Age-at-Death
text:
3 CLT Assumptions and Prediction
The draws are iid with finite variance. The unusual shape may make small-n sampling distributions depart from normality even though ordinary CLT conditions hold. I expect sample means to smooth the irregular population as n increases.

title: 08 · Extra Credit: Synthetic Age-at-Death
text:
5 Final Selected N and Interpretation

Code
report_selection(spec$id)

Selected N: n = 300

skewness: -0.0245
excess kurtosis: -0.0378
Q-Q RMSE: 0.0174
empirical SE: 1.5963
theoretical/reference SE: 1.5955 Evidence decision: The synthetic irregular mixture becomes stable by about n = 300, with near-zero shape diagnostics and empirical/theoretical SE agreement.

The selected value reflects the synthetic two-component discrete mixture supplied by the instructor. It is not historical mortality data; the irregular source shape is exactly what makes the fast stabilization of the sample mean worth checking.
